Benedict Arnold. One of the most capable and aggressive American commanders in the Revolutionary War, but also the man whose name became synonymous with treason in American history.

Arnold helped capture Fort Ticonderoga in 1775 and played a crucial role in the victory at Saratoga in 1777, which boosted American morale and secured French support. Yet he was passed over for promotion and recognition despite his military successes, growing resentful of Congress and the broader Revolutionary cause. Financial insolvency worsened his bitterness.

Beginning in 1779, Arnold secretly negotiated with British spy John André, eventually agreeing to surrender West Point, the fortress controlling the Hudson River, in exchange for money and a British commission. The plot was exposed when André was captured with incriminating documents. André was executed as a spy, but Arnold escaped to British lines.

He fought for the British in the remaining years of the war, but never regained the status or fortune he had hoped for. He died in obscurity in 1801, having fled to Canada and Britain after the war.

His name became a permanent epithet for betrayal in American culture. Calling someone "a Benedict Arnold" meant calling them a traitor.
